definition: Data annotation is the process within a dataset of adding relevant metadata labels or tags to enable machines to interpret the data in line with its intended use.
details: Data is a fundamental component in the development of artificial intelligence (AI). Data annotation allows AI models to interpret data. For example, it may inform the model that a particular set of pixels is a picture of a bicycle, or that a particular structure of sentence should be interpreted as a mathematical formula. Training AI models, particularly in computer vision and natural language processing, requires large volumes of annotated data. Annotation choices determine how machine learning algorithms recognize patterns and also drive the predictions they make. The dataset can take various forms, including images, text, audio files and video footage. Data annotation labels can be human-generated, system-generated, or a mix of both. The availability of large-scale annotated datasets has been a major factor in the development of modern artificial intelligence systems; particularly deep learning models that require vast quantities of labelled examples.

explainer.lead: Data annotation adds meaningful labels to raw data so an AI model can learn what the data represents. It matters because the examples and labels people provide shape the patterns a model recognizes and the predictions it makes.

tiers.eli5: Imagine sorting a big box of photos and putting a sticky note saying "bicycle" on each photo that contains one. Data annotation does something similar for computers, using pictures, writing, sound, or video. These notes help a computer learn what to look for next time.
tiers.practitioner: In computer vision and natural language processing, engineers prepare large volumes of images, text, audio, or video and attach labels through people, systems, or both. Label definitions and consistency need attention because annotation choices affect learned patterns and predictions; deep learning projects may also require vast labelled collections.
tiers.paperLevel: Formally, data annotation maps items in a dataset D to metadata labels relevant to an intended task, producing labelled examples for machine learning. Labels may be human-generated, system-generated, or mixed. A major practical constraint is scale: deep learning can require vast quantities of labelled examples, while annotation choices shape model behaviour.

explainer.example: For an image-recognition task, annotators label a set of pixels as a picture of a bicycle. The resulting labelled example helps the model learn visual patterns associated with bicycles.

usedIn.name: Computer vision
usedIn.detail: Labels connect visual content, such as pixels showing a bicycle, with its intended meaning.

usedIn.name: Natural language processing
usedIn.detail: Annotated text can indicate how a sentence or structure should be interpreted.

usedIn.name: Deep learning
usedIn.detail: Large collections of labelled examples support training modern deep learning models.

explainer.intuition: Raw data does not tell a model which parts matter for a task. Annotation supplies that missing meaning, turning examples into labelled material from which the model can learn.
howItWorks: Collect data such as images, text, audio, or video.
Choose labels suited to the intended use.
Attach labels using people, systems, or both.
Use the annotated examples to train a model.
The model learns patterns that guide its predictions.
explainer.whyItMatters: Training computer vision and natural language processing models requires large volumes of annotated data. Large-scale annotated datasets have been a major factor in modern AI, especially deep learning, and annotation choices directly influence what models learn.
misconceptions: It is not limited to images: text, audio, and video can be annotated too.
Labels need not be entirely human-made; systems can generate them, or both can contribute.
Annotation is not separate from model behaviour: label choices affect patterns and predictions.
